notes: How this part was researched: the session's shared web-search allowance was already spent (200 of 200) before this part's first search, so nothing here comes from a search engine. Every page was opened directly with the kit's honest User-Agent (states/net.py), one request at a time, through a small reader that reads a site's robots.txt first and obeys it: the campaign websites the candidates filed, each county's, city's and school district's own site (council and board minutes included), the two state parties' sites and local party units' own pages, the Legislative Reference Library, the Legislature's own site search and the state documents it holds, Wikipedia at its ordinary /wiki/ addresses, the University of Minnesota's election archive, and three news sites through their own pages (KAXE, the Fillmore County Journal, the Fairmont Sentinel). The pages were read on the evening of October 1, 2026 and in the first hours of October 2.

A find for the other parts, the judges above all: the Minnesota Legislative Manual 2025-2026 (the Blue Book, published by the Office of the Secretary of State) is held by the Legislative Reference Library at https://www.lrl.mn.gov/docs/2025/mandated/251328.pdf (24.8 MB; the kit's ballot/pdftext.py reads it). Pages 355 to 381 of the PDF list every district judge by district, in order of seniority, with the seat number in parentheses, the appointment date and the election years; pages 401 to 429 list every county's officers with the year each term expires; and pages 509 to 575 give the 2024 general election results by House district, with the party of every legislative and congressional candidate. Both judges of this part, Mark Larson, Brian Swedberg and three 2024 runs rest on it. The Library's site was reached through the Legislature's own site search (the page https://www.leg.mn.gov/search.aspx fetches https://www.leg.mn.gov/search_functions.aspx?q=...&q_all=...&default=AND&c=full, and answers in JSON), which also finds the Governors' archived appointment releases; the Minnesota Judicial Branch's own site was not asked at all.

A stricter line on robots.txt than some earlier parts took, because this sweep is run by Claude: a page was read only when the site's robots.txt lets in both the kit's reader and Anthropic's agents by name (ClaudeBot, Claude-User, Claude-SearchBot, anthropic-ai, Claude-Web), as part 16 did for one campaign site. That closed the hometownsource.com papers (the Caledonia Argus among them), southernminn.com (the Faribault Daily News), presspubs.com (the Shoreview Press) and the Voice of Alexandria, whose robots.txt lets the kit's reader in but turns ClaudeBot, anthropic-ai and Claude-Web away, as well as the Forum Communications papers. Nothing was read on them, so a few start years those papers probably report are missing here (see the last note).

The campaign websites the candidates filed were learned by running the kit's own step (python -m ballot.local_sites files) on a scratch copy of the database; the real database was only read. Fourteen of this part's thirty candidates filed one. Thirteen were opened and read and are listed below with what ties each to the race. The fourteenth, Tad Jude's tadjude.com, answered the reader with a redirect to a CAPTCHA page, so it was not read and is a review item, not a website finding. Two filed addresses lead to another name: sebastianformayor.com to www.sebastianforwoodbury.com, and www.calebformn.com to calebformn.com (three more only add www); the filed address is the one given, so the loader sees it as the filed one. Likely campaign addresses for candidates who filed none were tried only by asking whether the name has an address on the network; none led to a campaign site that could be read (joeatkins.com returns an empty page; daltonswanson.com asks every script to stay out and is not known to be the candidate's; edpaschke.com was not opened, since a well-known painter had that name).

Not read, and nothing worked around: tadjude.com (a CAPTCHA redirect); the Minnesota Judicial Branch's site and the state's mn.gov pages (a bot wall and a CAPTCHA to this machine, by the earlier parts' reports; not requested at all), so neither judge has an official page here; Clearwater County's site (its robots.txt asks every unlisted script to stay out), so Mark Larson has no official page and his office rests on the Legislative Manual; Houston County's site (the secure handshake fails at one address and the other does not answer), so Brian Swedberg has none either; the Crookston Times (robots.txt keeps everyone out) and KROX radio's site search (HTTP 403); the Senate District 29 DFL's site (no answer) and the Senate District 47 DFL's (a certificate the reader would not accept). A published spreadsheet of candidates that the Rock Ridge district links to was not opened, since such lists carry contact columns.

For the second reader. (a) Chris Swanson of Cloquet is not the Chris Swanson who was mayor of Two Harbors: his own site says he was born and raised in Cloquet and has served 'on the Cloquet City Council for Wards 3 and 1', KAXE's House District 11A guide gives his community as Cloquet and quotes him on his work 'as a Cloquet City Councilor', and the City of Cloquet lists him as Councilor Ward 1. His offices are dated from the city's own council minutes: appointed to Ward 3 on July 16, 2019; the canvass in the minutes of November 15, 2022 shows him elected again in Ward 3, while the same minutes already speak of the Ward 3 vacancy and the minutes of December 6 and 20, 2022 no longer list him, so his Ward 3 service is ended at 2022; he took the oath for Ward 1 on March 18, 2025, when the council also named him to the seat on the Cloquet Area Fire District Board that a council member had held. That board seat came with the council seat and no page read says whether he holds it today, so it has no end; the second reader may prefer to drop it, as part 1 dropped a seat held as part of a council term. (b) Tad Jude: the Hennepin County commissioner's start (1989) is the Legislative Reference Library's, which leaves the end as '19??'; the end year 1993 is Wikipedia's, citing Ballotpedia. Wikipedia's opening paragraph says he was a district judge 'from 2001 to 2011', which its own later paragraph (elected 2010, re-elected 2016, ten years on the bench) and the Library (01/2011 to 01/2022) contradict; the Library's years are the ones recorded. His earlier runs under a party label come from the Library where it names the party, from the University of Minnesota's election archive for the 1992 primary and the 1996 general election (a university archive of returns, not a news organization; marked secondary as other parts mark it), from Wikipedia for the 2022 attorney general's race, and from the Legislative Manual for 2024. His first House election, in 1972, was nonpartisan, so the first entry is dated 1974, the first election the Library records under the DFL label. His 2022 run for Hennepin County Attorney was for a nonpartisan office and is not a finding. The party's name from 1975 to 1995 was Independent-Republican, and is written that way. (c) Joe Atkins: the tie between the commissioner and the former legislator is stated on both sides: the Library's record lists 'Dakota County, Minnesota (County Commissioner); 2017 to ?', and the county's background sheet says he was mayor of Inver Grove Heights for ten years and a state legislator before joining the county board. (d) Steven J. Heinen: Benton County's pages write Steve Heinen and give no starting year; the start year 2019 rests on the county board's minutes (not among the commissioners on December 18, 2018; among them on January 8, 2019, the first meeting of the year). (e) The two judges: the Legislative Manual gives 'Appointed December 18, 2017. Elected 2020.' for Sophia Y. Vuelo (seat 15) and 'Appointed April 7, 2006. Elected 2008, 2014, 2020.' for Tamara L. Yon (seat 15); the seat numbers match the two races. The Governors' releases announcing the appointments are dated a little earlier (November 30, 2017 and January 20, 2006) and are given in the source text; Wikipedia, citing the Star Tribune, says Judge Vuelo was sworn in on January 4, 2018. Wikipedia gives her birth as '1971 or 1972', which is not a year, and the 2006 release gives Judge Yon's age, so no birth year is recorded for either. (f) Mark Larson and Brian Swedberg: the Legislative Manual lists each with a term that expires in 2027 and no starting year. 'to' is written 'now' for both on the strength of that term; for the sheriff a newspaper item of August 10, 2026 says so as well, for Mark Larson no page of 2026 was read, and the second reader may prefer to leave his end blank. (g) Alison Sherman: the Stillwater district's page gives 'First elected: 11/2020' for her where it gives January dates for members who won regular elections (1/2021, 1/2023, 1/2025) and 'Appointed: 4/2023' for an appointee, so the column reads as the month a member joined the board, and her 'from' is written '2020'; her own site says only that she 'was elected to the Stillwater Area School Board in 2020'. (h) Cathy Nathan: 'elected 2018' is an election year (her own site: 'elected to the Rochester Public School Board in 2018 and 2022'), not a start year. (i) Jessica Schwinn's start year (sworn in January 2023) and Kyle Coryell's (appointed January 2025) are stated in so many words, the first on her own site and the second on the city's page. (j) John Sebastian's site never gives his first name on the pages read; it is the address he filed, it is about the Woodbury mayor's race, and it speaks of 'both mayoral candidates', of whom our list has two. (k) Caleb Steffenhagen's site carries no year on the pages read; it is the address he filed, and the Carver County Republican Party's 2026 page links to it as his campaign website. (l) Aric Putnam is a sitting member with a roster record, so only his website and endorsements are given; the Library's record of him agrees with the roster's birth date.

party_support (a key the loader does not read, in the shape parts 0, 5, 6, 10 and 12 use): two listings where a party unit publishes its backing of a candidate for a nonpartisan office under a heading that is not the word endorsement. The Senate District 34 DFL lists Stacey Yurcek under 'Letter of Support Candidates' (part 5 records the same page for another candidate). The Olmsted 20/24 DFL's '2026 DFL Voting Guide' lists Cathy Nathan among its recommendations for the Rochester school board. They are kept apart from endorsed_by so that no page calls them endorsements; whether and how they are shown is John's decision.

Party endorsements: the Minnesota DFL's list of endorsed candidates names Aric Putnam, Karla Hult, Chris Swanson and Colton Kratky; the Senate District 14 and Senate District 50 units publish their own lists too. Our list shows a contested DFL primary on August 11 in Karla Hult's and Colton Kratky's races; the pages read list both as endorsed today and do not say when the endorsement was given. For the Republicans, the state party published its endorsement of Tad Jude on May 29, 2026, and the Carver County Republican Party lists Caleb Steffenhagen under 'Endorsed MN House and Senate Candidates' (it also lists Tad Jude under 'State-Wide Endorsed Candidates', which is not recorded a second time). The party pages that could be read for the nonpartisan candidates (the Senate District 43, 33, 32 and 19 DFL units, the Clay County Republicans, the St. Louis County Republicans' 2026 list, the Olmsted County Republicans' September newsletter) name none of this part's other candidates; the Clay County DFL's and Senate District 41 DFL's pages are drawn by script and showed no names.

Read and left out on purpose: an age on Election Day (KAXE gives Chris Swanson's) and an age in an appointment release, neither of which fixes a birth year; employment; schools and degrees; nonprofit, association and church boards; labor and other non-party endorsements; what candidates said at forums; and the family and religion lines of the Legislative Reference Library's records and of the Governors' releases. Advisory seats were left out as well, since no page read shows them to be offices one is elected or appointed to in the usual sense: Stacey Yurcek's seat on the Osseo district's District Planning Advisory Council (the district says membership 'is based on interest' and lasts a year), Sophia Vuelo's past membership of the Saint Paul-Ramsey County Community Health Services Advisory Committee (her own site, no years), and Chris Swanson's time on Cloquet's Citizens Advisory Board and as the council's liaison to its Library Board. Committee seats that come with a school board or council seat were not listed either. The affidavits of candidacy and campaign finance reports the City of Moorhead posts were not opened.

Nothing a card may show was found for six candidates, who are listed with no findings. Nathanael S. Landsteiner and Edward (Ed) Paschke: the City of Fairmont's council page and its nine board and commission pages name neither, and the Fairmont Sentinel's report of the mayoral forum (October 1, 2026) names no public office or campaign website for Landsteiner. Christine Thompson: Shoreview's list of council members and its nine committee and commission pages do not name her. Dalton Swanson: the City of Moorhead lists him as a Ward 1 candidate and none of its eleven board and commission pages names him. Jessica Ruehling: the Crosby-Ironton district's page lists six sitting board members and she is not one of them. Alan Sherek: KAXE's Rock Ridge School District guide says it received no response from him and does not list him among the sitting members. The Legislature's site search finds no state document that says anything a card may show about any of the six. A second pass with the search tool would be worth it for them.

Start years still missing for sitting officials whose own government names the office but not when it began: Charlie Meyer (Douglas County's posted minutes go back only to 2022), Mark Larson, Kit Johnson, Damain D. Sandy, John Rowan, Corinne Hennen (the Jordan district's profile pages open only by script) and Brian Swedberg (the Fillmore County Journal reported his candidacy in May 2022, when he was not yet sheriff; no page read says when he took office). The Legislature's site search shows which editions of the Legislative Manual name each county officer, which would bracket a start between two editions, but an edition is not a start year and none was taken from it.

verifier_notes: Every address in the candidates' findings was opened again on October 2, 2026 with the kit's honest User-Agent (states/net.py), 55 pages and PDFs in all, each answered on the first try; PDFs (the Legislative Manual, Cloquet and Benton County minutes, the Dakota County background sheet, the Olmsted DFL voting guide) were read with ballot/pdftext.py. tadjude.com was not requested: the researcher met a CAPTCHA there, and the review item rests on the two party pages that link to it, which were re-opened and do link to it.

The thirteen filed websites were checked against the Secretary of State's list by running the kit's own step on an in-memory copy of the database (the real database was only read): each address is the one filed for that race and name.

Same person: every finding is tied to its race by the place and the office (our record's district or seat number matches the page: Dakota 2, Benton 3, Douglas 4, Clearwater 5, judges' seat 15 in the Second and Ninth Districts). Chris Swanson's Cloquet offices rest on his own campaign site (Cloquet City Council, Wards 3 and 1; the Fire District Board) together with the city's page and minutes. Joe Atkins the commissioner and Joe Atkins the former legislator are tied by the Library's record and the county's background sheet.

Kept as recorded though inferred from two official pages rather than stated in one: Steven J. Heinen's start in 2019 (absent from the minutes of December 18, 2018, present on January 8, 2019) and the end of Chris Swanson's Ward 3 service in 2022. The Cloquet Area Fire District Board seat is kept with no end, as the minutes record the appointment and his own site lists the board.
